title: GeoMIND: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in Robotic Manipulation
claim: A benchmark organizes its task families along two diagnostic dimensions, with concrete example instances surrounding the taxonomy.
layout: Central 2-axis taxonomy grid with six example panels around it, connected by lines
description: A central 2-D chart titled 'Two Core Dimensions of Embodied Spatial Understanding' has the y-axis Spatial Memory and the x-axis Spatial Reasoning, each running low to high. A large gradient 'GeoMind' wordmark sits in the middle. Six rounded task-family labels fill the grid: Scene Updating, Identity Tracking, Geometric Inference, Target Identification, Relational Grounding and Constraint Composition. Thin colored lines link each label to a surrounding dashed-border example panel. Each panel shows three simulated robot-arm renders (Initial State, Robot trajectory, Ground Truth), with pink boxes and black arrows marking targets and motion. A natural-language instruction in monospace sits under each, for example 'Pick up the block left of the bowl.' Panels sit on the left, right and bottom. The eye goes first to the GeoMind title and the grid.
caption: Overview of GEOMIND. GEOMIND organizes structured spatial understanding along two diagnostic dimensions: spatial memory and spatial reasoning. The six task families cover different combinations of these dimensions. Surrounding examples illustrate how GEOMIND couples spatial instructions with structured object layouts and scene changes. The instructions are illustrative; evaluated actions and success criteria are specified in Appendix D.
abstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.
